utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Gotovina et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Repinc, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. And if Mr. Mikulicic is ready, he'll now continue his examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll carry on where we left off yesterday, which is the events related to the liberation of Donji Lapac. And for that purpose, may I have 3D00652 called up, please. In paragraph 153 of your expert report, you state -- or, rather, you quote this document, which relates to footnote 103, which is a report from the Gospic Military District in which it is stated that at around 1800 hours, the units of the Gospic Military District, in collaboration with special MUP units, liberated the town of Donji Lapac. And then in the last sentence of that first paragraph, in addition, it says that the units were deployed in a mopping-up operation of the terrain, the clearing of the front, and the collection of war booty. Now, faced with a situation where a new area was being liberated, in the military sense, is it customary for a unit, after having liberated an area, to mop up the terrain, to sanitise the area, and to collect war booty? And when you considered your documents, did you see that in Donji Lapac the special police went about this duty, in addition to the military?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As this -- in the way that this document was written, the clearing of the terrain, sanitisation, collection of war booty, was carried out in the Military District of Gospic, and that can but need not include Donji Lapac. But, in any event, the unit which is attacking and taking control of a certain area, unless it is facing frontwards, can carry out these activities with the aim of ensuring that there are no stragglers -- enemy straggler forces which could in any way be a threat to the military in the area. Now, usually the clearing of the terrain would be conducted by other echelons or reserve forces and not the forces who launched the attack and were facing frontward, whether they were taking control of the defence line and waiting for a continuation of combat activities. Now, as far as the special police is concerned, I did not see any mention of a clearing Lapac as a town. What was said was that the town of Lapac had been taken control of and that the forces were moving further towards the border or, rather, the area around Kulin Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have a number, Mr. President, for this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D1924. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1924 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could I now have document 65 ter 00986 called up, please, which is a document which you quote once again in your expert report in footnote 109. And it is an intelligence report for the Split Military District for the 7th of August, 1995. As I was saying, 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I'm informed, and of course I don't know all the 65 ter numbers by heart, that this is a document which is already admitted into evidence as a confidential document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of it, Your Honours. Then we could go to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, or -- I do not know what's the reason, I do not know what the document is. But perhaps out of an abundance of caution, we go into private session and look at the document first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: General, the document you refer to in footnote 109, and -- I'd like to draw your attention to the middle part of that document, where it says that the units in their advance were linked up and taken control of the Krupa area and were continuing with the clearing of the area around Velebit, while the units of the special police of MUP had reached the following positions, and then it stipulates what those positions are. Now, General, sir, in this document we can also see that the units of the Croatian Army, in their advance, are carrying out clearing operations of the terrain. Does that follow on from what you said when you were commenting on the previous document? Is this the same case, or is it a different case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that we're going to talk about the problems of clearing the terrain or search of the terrain, I would put it that way, because I personally consider that the way in which the term "ciscenje" or "clearing" was used does not actually correspond to the actual definition of clearing or cleansing according to the normal tactical explanations given. So there are many documents in which "clearing" is referred to, "search" is referred to either as both terms used together or one term or another term used, so we can determine what is what here. And I would say that in this case, the units in the area which remained behind the lines that were reached were quite simply searched. They searched the area in order not to confront any enemy forces, but possibly to see that groups hadn't been infiltrated, or things of that kind, and to search and discover minefields, equipment that had remained behind, and anything that could hinder normal movement and life -- the life of the forces on the liberated area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May this document be assigned an number, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, could we ask the witness -- he interprets what it most likely would have been, what the factual basis for such a conclusion is, apart from what we -- the factual circumstances at that moment. Could you tell us what makes you -- what factual information makes you conclude as you described it in your last answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we look at the tactical definitions of certain activities which units carry out during an "hors de combat", then "clearing" is a special operation with a special aim, and the aim of mop-up or clearing is to uncover the enemy; not small forces, but large-scale enemy forces in front of you, and then to clear the area completely of all forces which in any way can jeopardise the activities of the units in their advance. But that is not the kind of activity that went on here. What went on here is that the area had already been liberated, which meant cleansed, already, so they didn't expect to come across any enemy forces of that kind. What they wanted to do here was to establish possible contact with the remaining forces, and then they would decide, depending on what was going on when contacts were established and what those forces were, then they would decide what kind of activities they would take on, whether clearing or cleansing activities, or an attack, or some other activities to surround the area, or whatever. So this clearing or mop-up is an operation which, from the very beginning, has its goal. That is to say, in a certain area, what was wanted was to clear all the possible forces that were there and to ensure that the forces who were there in the area had the freedom of action without coming under threat or without jeopardy from the adversary, from the enemy. I'd like to mention, in particular, that this cleansing or clearing is not something which was a side-effect. It wasn't any side-effect or auxiliary action that happened in order to effect an attack, but it was an activity from the very beginning which was an aim in itself. And in this particular case, when the terrain was searched, the goal was not to enter into any major combat with the enemy, but the search was conducted according to certain rules or, rather, methods whereby all the forces, infantry and anything else, artillery, are not brought in for any major fighting, whereas this is a normal activity in a cleansing whereby -- or clearing whereby all the members are involved in the clearing of a certain area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I must admit that your answer is not entirely clear to me. On the one hand, you say the area was liberated. I think the document says that it was, and, therefore, there was no organised resistance anymore to be expected. Now, what, then -- minefields is clear to me, but would there be individual remaining combatants, or what exactly -- now you said there were certain methods, there were certain goals. What exactly was that, apart from the minefields? That's clear. I can imagine that you search for weapon depots. But as far as military resistance is concerned, what would you expect and what were you looking for, at least to the extent you know, because your answer was quite abstract? But do you have any knowledge, specifically, on this action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely what you've just said. The area had been liberated, and since it was liberated territory, that meant that you couldn't find any large organised forces there. There wouldn't have been any there which needed to be cleansed. So cleansing is an activity that happens in combat, combat operations. Now, let's take, for example, that a unit has been given an assignment in its attack to carry out a certain manoeuvre. Then that unit can be assigned individual tasks within that general manoeuvre. It can receive the task of neutralising a certain area, it can be given the assignment of breaking through a certain line, or the assignment can be to encircle a certain region, or it can be given an assignment to clear a certain area. If it has received an assignment to clear a certain area, that means an area in front of it, then in that sense it will have to clear that area of all forces. However, here the activities that were carried out after -- subsequent to the line having been broken through and after the enemy had been pushed back, what was happening in the rear was no longer a cleansing operation, but was just a search of the terrain. And the search of the terrain was conducted in order to find and uncover and possibly neutralise and capture, or push back, or force certain smaller organised or non-organised groups to flee, and that also included uncovering any remaining weapons, or equipment, or depots, ammunition depots and other depots, and it also had the aim of uncovering and recording and reporting any remaining individuals, stragglers who had remained in the area, and then taking care of that for people to be able to continue their lives normally. So the object of the search was to see that in the area, after the enemy had withdrawn, to prevent any cases of anyone coming across something and taking anything that they should not have taken, to suffer because of that, and that nobody had taken care of this and given assistance to the people there and recorded all these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking you this question because on the previous document, although not highlighted, we see - and I know that it was the Gospic Military District - that the report of what happened resulted in the arrest of five conscripts and, I think, seventeen civilians, so I'm wondering what exactly, in terms of searching for persons, what this mopping up could mean. Do you know the result of this mopping-up exercise, because this is an intelligence report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, many of the reports that were sent out at that time said that the units were conducting a mop-up operation or a clearing of the terrain. In certain places, it says "ciscenje." In others it says "pretraga," "search." Now, my point is that the way in which the Military District of Gospic, in its report, said that it had conducted a search of -- a clearing of the terrain, did not correspond to the tactical concept and notion of "ciscenje," of cleansing, clearing, or mop-up. It would be more precise if the Military District of Gospic had carried out a search of the terrain, "pretres" or "pretraga," with the aim of carrying out these activities; that is to say, to uncover not only equipment, but also individuals in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Including civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as civilians are concerned, it is normal that -- and this can be seen later on from the subsequent reports of the special police, that during the search operation the civilians that they came across in the villages were recorded, their names were recorded, and they checked out to see whether they had already been registered by some other services active in the area with the aim of providing them with the necessary assistance to carry on their lives in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think in the previous report, it reported that 17 civilians were arrested, and I have some difficulties in reconciling your description of what kind of care was given to civilians and what is reported in that -- again, it was the Gospic Military District, but what was described in that report. Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could have an exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D1925. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1925 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As a follow-up on this topic that we intended to go back to, but since it's been raised, can we look at 3D00581, which is a report of the military police where you, General -- which you referred to in footnote 111 and 112, and that's in paragraph 163 of your expert report. It is a report of the 71st MP Battalion which states that on the 7th of August, the MP Platoon was set up and began its activity in Gracac. However, I'd like to focus on page 2 of the document, and in particular item 6, which states: "The search of the terrain was conducted in the area of Hinic at the junction leading to Doljani, with a view to finding two unknown persons which had, at 9.00, opened small-arms fire at members of the 4/2 Company of the Military Police and fled in the direction of Doljani." General, sir, this search of the terrain referred to in this MP report, can it in any way enlighten us in terms of the definition of the search or the clearing of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that members of the military police, as well as members of the special police, in view of the type of weapons and equipment they had, would fall under the category of light infantry, in view of the fact that this was the sort of units they were, they were not able to carry out mop-up operations, because in that case it would mean or involve engaging stronger enemy forces which cannot be attacked in the formation which is usually employed in a search or in a mop-up operation, be it an individual next to an individual along the defence line, or a unit next to a unit, where an attack is launched and the units advance to a certain line, where the search ends.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be assigned a number, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D1926. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1926 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at paragraph 164 of your expert report, and item 8.5, which refers to the activities on the 8th of August, 1995. In paragraph 165, you state that the joint special police forces reinforced their defence at the lines reached and that one battalion of the special police reinforced the area and extended the line towards Kulin Vakuf by occupying the villages of Kalati [phoen] and Zagorje, where preparations were made to relinquish their positions at the state borders -- border to the units of the Gospic and Split military districts, as ordered by the chief of the Main Staff of the Croatian Army. Can you please comment on this tactical task of taking up the state border, that's to say reaching the state border, the task given to the special police, and then the holding of the line reached at the state border? Was this something that also fell within the purview of the special police, or was it, in fact, within the purview of some other units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole operation was directed towards reaching the state border, at which point conditions were to be created for the normalisation of life of the inhabitants of the liberated area. As far as capturing a certain area goes, this means that certain units reached a line and switched to defence in order to defend the area until the arrival of the units which would take that task on from there. The special police could be given this sort of task, but was not, in view of the fact that this was not within the scope of work of the special police, as it were, to defend a certain area for a prolonged period of time. This sort of task is normally handed over to the military, and the special police goes on to carry out duties inherent to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us look at document 3D00803, which you refer to in paragraph 170, in footnote 119. This is a report pertaining to the execution of tasks by the 71st Military Police Battalion in the combat zone and the newly-liberated areas. It follows from the document that on the 8th of August, an MP platoon was set up in Donji Lapac which set about performing its tasks. Let us look at page 2 of the document, item 6, where it is stated that the military police, which is the one that made the document, carried out the searches of the terrain in Udbina and Donji Lapac. As soon as the HV units arrived, certain events were recorded. General, the tasks performed by the special police, as per this report, is it within the definition that you gave of the search of the terrain, or is it a different situation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this involves the military police, I would say that this is a customary task that the military police would receive in that period of time; i.e., the search of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can the document be given a number?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D1927. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us turn to the activities on the 9th of August which you describe in Chapter 8.6, starting from paragraph 172. In paragraph 173, you state that the joint special police forces of MUP turned over the border in the territory of Gornji and Donji Lapac to the units of the Gospic Military District, and the Joint Forces Staff received an order from the chief of the Main Staff for a new task indicating a new stage in the activity of joint special police forces; that's to say, transition from offensive combat operations to clearing and search of the terrain in the area of Petrova Gora. To this end, can -- or on this issue, can you give us your comments concerning the way in which the state border was handed over to others for care and the way in which the special police was given a new order by the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way the special police handed over the control over the state border to the Gospic Military District was recorded in this report, and this was in accordance with the orders of the Main Staff concerning the division of responsibilities between the Split Military District and Gospic Military District, in relation to the border that was established on the 6th of August, 1995. The area where special police forces were deployed which reached the border was within the area of responsibility of the Gospic Military District. As for the order which General Markac received, let me be quite precise and say that General Markac received the order. However, the order, itself, did not contain a clearly-defined task of the special police. Rather, it stated that what was to come next was the securing of the area and activities of blocking Petrova Gora. Since the chief of the Main Staff had also sent the order to the commander of the special police force, even though the latter did not receive a task therein, I would say -- my conclusion would be that this was a sort of a preparatory order or something that was to be an indication to General Markac of the fact that his forces might also be involved in such an activity; that's to say, in the conduct of the search, blocking, and clearing, if necessary, of a certain area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, for your answer. We will go back to that topic a bit later. First, however, we should look together at document 3D00735, which you refer to in footnote 122, which is related to paragraph 172. It is a letter sent from the Special Police Staff in Seline on 10th of August to the Intelligence Administration of the Main Staff of the Croatian Army by Petar Ricko, the commander that you already referred to. Let's look at the last paragraph, which states: "On the 10th of August, forces of the special police of the MUP will be engaged on tasks of searching and mopping up of the terrain in the general area of Medak to find and destroy remaining IDS, reconnaissance and sabotage groups. Over the past few days, small enemy groups opened infantry fire on members of the ordinary police of the Ministry of the Interior engaged on securing the Gospic-Gracac road." General, sir, the task of the special police which Major Petar Ricko announces to the Main Staff clearly indicates that there were straggling enemy groups present. Is this an adequate way of responding to this sort of security-related situation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If at the time there were several reports indicating that there was a threat and, indeed, fire opened on members of the uniformed police and members of the armed forces, in this particular case it involved an area that was liberated in the course of the 5th of August, evidently there were remaining groups or individuals present in the area. And since the threat was such that it made the normal activity and movement of persons impossible and was life-threatening, it was necessary for the area to be searched and such individuals or groups either uncovered or forced to withdraw from the area. Normally, the role of a search operation should be, whenever possible, for such individuals to be uncovered and neutralised. I repeat, however, the search operation need not necessarily involve this element as well. If the adversary does not engage in combat, this probably means that the force will withdraw in the face of the forces involved in the search operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can this document be assigned a number, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D1928.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1928 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, after the combat operations in which the special police took part of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia, that is, I'm now going to move on to a section in your expert report, to Chapter 9, "Activities of the Special Police units in the clearing and searching of the terrain. In paragraph 176, you say that after Operation Storm was completed, that the special police forces, as of the 9th of August, 1995 -- concluding with the 9th of August, 1995, withdrew from the border zone of the Republic of Croatia along the Una River and that the positions were taken over by the forces of the Gospic Military District and regrouped their forces to prepare for subsequent missions, and to allow rest time for personnel. And after that, you refer to the fact that the focus was shifted from classical combat missions to clear-up or mop-up operations and search operations. Now, General, sir, you've already told us something about -- or, rather, you defined what, in your view, a mop-up operation means and what a search operation means. However, this Trial Chamber from numerous documents has seen previously that these two notions, these two concepts even in the same document are used parallelly, simultaneously. And in your expert report, you say that it would appear that they are used as synonyms. However, could you explain that to us a little bit? Are they really synonyms, or should one differentiate between the two concepts as you have defined them? Or, rather, how do you explain the fact that in documents these terms were used in different contexts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I have already explained this, explained the basic difference, the fundamental difference, and it can be illustrated best perhaps taking the example of a clearing -- the mop-up operation of Petrova Gora and comparing that to the search of the terrain which was conducted in other parts. Now, in what sense? If we analyse the documents which General Markac, as the commander of the operation -- of the mop-up operation of Petrova Gora, the assignment he was given, then we can see from those documents that the first area -- initially, the area of Petrova Gora had not been liberated, or, rather, the forces of the Croatian Army were still at the foot of or the approaches to Mount Petrova Gora. Now, why this is a mop-up operation is illustrated in the fact that General Markac, as the commander of that particular operation, had been given a series of units, guards units -- ranging from guards units to brigades of the Croatian Army, with all the necessary equipment and weapons and armoured weapons, it was a large-scale operation, the goal of which was that all the forces should be set in motion frontally to clear up the whole area so that all the forces that were found there should be completely neutralised, encircled, captured, and forced to surrender or to withdraw across the state border. On the other hand - I've already mentioned this - activities -- search activities were conducted in an area that was already liberated. So if I were to draw a parallel and make a comparison, I would say that what happened was this: There was a situation by which after Petrova Gora had been cleansed from the 12th to the 14th, let's say, of August, 1995, that the special police, sometime after that date, was given the assignment of going to Petrova Gora once again -- or had it gone to Petrova Gora once again, it wouldn't have been a cleansing operation; it would have conducted a search operation of the Petrova Gora area. So that's that example. Now, as regards to the problems that occur when different concepts or notions are used, these problems arise first of all because the Croatian Army at that time still did not have a well-defined doctrine, and if it didn't have a doctrine, it couldn't have had definitions for a series of other elements; first and foremost, the concepts of war skills or combat skills, or certain concepts which would clearly establish what is what and differentiate between what is what. So there were no official definitions stating that a mop-up operation or clear-up operation is one thing, and a search operation is another thing. There was scope for inertia here, so people used similar things that could imply similar things understood by individuals who were in charge of carrying out certain activities. So for most people, clear-up or mop-up or search was one and the same thing, whereas in actual fact they were different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at document 3D00904. You refer to this document in footnote 137 or paragraph 183, where you explain searches of the terrain. Now, this action is described in a manual entitled "Command and Military Tactics in the Police," or "Combat Tactics in the Police," a manual issued by the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia, and it defines a search of the terrain as an organised, systematic search of certain areas and terrains and any facilities on it in order to detect the presence and position of the enemy or traces which would indicate his location and establishing combat contact. Now, this definition is to be found on page 3D05-0703 of the Croatian version, and this entire activity is explained there. Now, General, since this activity, search of the terrain, is contained and defined in the manual for police, the police, and police conduct, could you comment on it? Can you tell us, is it a police activity and police method, and not a military one? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether we can make this distinction or not, can we say that the military units cannot conduct a search of the terrain, that would be wrong. I don't think we could say that, because if we envisage a situation, certain states that do not have a special police to deal with activities of this kind, in that case the military forces would conduct searches of the terrain, as is the case within -- as is the case for all the activities under -- after Operation Storm. It was established that it wasn't only the special police forces that searched the terrain, but that the military police did that too, and that other units engaged in that as well, other units who were in that -- which were in that area. Now, what is important here -- it is important to stress the following in this context : Within the remit of the work of the special police, one of the most important tasks is to fight sabotage, diversion, regroups, but also to resolve certain situations of hostages, involving hostages. And the special police was, therefore, used to search the terrain, searching for the perpetrators of crimes and criminal acts. And I should like to mention that that context that the police, as an organisation, especially the special police, as far as the search of the terrain is concerned, this was a natural, routine activity on their part for which they were well trained and had to be well trained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May a number be assigned to this document, please, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D1929. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 186 of your expert report, you say that the special police had certain training sessions with respect to the search of the terrain. May we have your comments on that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, within the frameworks of the training courses that were conducted at the Training Centre at Kofrcan, as part of the training plan and programme, under the subject of police tactics, one of the subtopics was searches, search of the terrain, and 10 hours were devoted to that subject, which means that it was an important one. This training involved theoretical aspects and practical training, and all the trainees were given a form or format telling them in what way an order was written when assignments were given to search the terrain. So they had to know how this document was compiled and in what way a search was conducted as a separate activity that they were assigned to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, let's go back to a topic you've already broached, General. We'll go through it very quickly, and it is the mop-up and search of Petrova Gora, the terrain there. In paragraph 189, you say that the chief of the Main Staff, on the 10th of August, issued an order by which Lieutenant General Mladen Markac was assigned a mission, a particular mission, and then you go on to quote what that mission was. And I'd just like to say for the Trial Chamber it is Exhibit 1103 that we're talking about here. And then further on in paragraph 192, you go on to say that in compliance with this assignment, the special MUP forces from Northern Dalmatia and Lika, and those that were on leave from their core police departments, were transferred to the Petrova Gora area, which is geographically located outside Sector South, in which up until then the special police joint forces or collective forces operated there until -- and remained there until the 21st of August. General, the action carried out by the special police units outside Sector South in the mop-up operation of Petrova Gora was an action following an order from the chief of the Main Staff. Please correct me if I'm wrong, but does that mean that throughout that time the special police continued, although it was pulled out of Sector South, remained and continued to be under the command of the Main Staff of the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The orders issued by General -- or the orders received by General Markac, if we look at them, then it was quite obvious that the special police was still in the chain of the command of the chief of the Main Staff and that the chief of the Main Staff was still supervising, ordering the work and functioning of the special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, starting out from the 21st of August, and we find that in paragraph 198 of your report, the search operations started in the area of Lika and Northern Dalmatia and also outside Sector South. So the special police, if I can put it this way, returns on the 21st of August to Sector South. And here, once again, in footnote 155, you quote an order from the chief of the Main Staff - for the Trial Chamber's reference, it is Exhibit D559 - in which the tasks are defined for members of the special police. In section B in that same paragraph 198, it says that the task was: Destroy remaining hostile formations in clearing terrain. Now, in paragraph F of that same order, reference is made to the fact that the training of war structures in units through a cycle of preparation and replacements to safe-guard state borders and conduct a field search. Once again, we see in one and the same document, two terms are used, "clearing" and "searching." Is that in keeping with what you told us earlier?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this demonstrates that precisely. It just shows that if today, for example, I could ask the author of the document what they meant by "clearing" and what they meant by "search," I'm not sure that they could give me a clear-cut answer and distinguish between the two terms, as they are used and written down here and as was implemented on the ground faced with the situation, because in my understanding of the situation, after the 14th of August, when this order was issued in the area, that is to say on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, not a single operation of mop-up or clearing of the terrain was conducted as defined by certain combat rules; first of all, the rules of the American Army and NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now a question staying with that topic, General. What was the situation like, on the basis of your study of the documents, that provoked the chief of the Main Staff to issue an order about clearing and searching the terrains, starting with the 24th of August in Sector South, once again? What was the motive?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 21st of August, interpreter's correction, 21st of August.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what we can see from certain reports that the military district sent in to the chief of the Main Staff of the operations headquarters, in the area there was still attacks going on, instances of attack against certain members of the armed forces and the police, and some of them resulted in fatalities. So faced with a situation of this kind, the chief of the Main Staff quite obviously made the conclusion that it was necessary to secure that whole area or, rather, to prevent such activities on the part of the enemy and to create conditions for normal life and work for everyone in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, let's look at document 3D00226 in that context, to which you refer in footnote 158. And it is an extraordinary report sent out by the Command of the Gospic Military District to the Ministry of Defence, in which it says that persons had been killed -- or, rather, that one reserve soldier had been killed on the 12th of August and that at around 230 hours two members of the 8th Home Guards Regiment were killed, and that this killing came about when a small group of Chetniks probably entered the village and moved around the local village road, and that the soldiers who were killed were on the job securing the road. So was this a report about the lack of security and safety that still existed in this newly-liberated area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and there's nothing in particular that can be added to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can this document be assigned a number, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D1930. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1930 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us look at another document on this same subject; namely, 3D00597, which you refer to in footnote 157. This is again a report to the Intelligence Administration of the Main Staff of the Croatian Army by the Gospic Military District Command, which states that in the area of Medak, by a straggling enemy group, members of the Ministry of the Interior were fired upon from infantry weapons. And according to the information available at the time, four policemen were wounded, four military policemen. Again, this document relates to what you discussed, and that's the security situation which was still very unstable following the liberation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can a number be given to the document, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we decide on the matter, Mr. Mikulicic, apparently there was a problem in the Medak area. What's the relevance to here and there, pick out from areas which apparently are not in Sector South? I mean, that the country was not quiet seems to be -- well, seems to be -- I don't know whether there's any dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honour, Medak area is in Sector South, in fact, it's part of the Sector South. This is on the road which leads from Gospic to Gracac, and it's, let's say, about 35 to 40 kilometres from Gracac to the north-west.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just then look, because earlier the Petrova Gora was outside of Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I may have mixed up matters, that you switched from outside Sector South, now you're inside. Could you then precisely define, then -- let me just have a look. Petrova Gora is well north of Sector South?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Petrova Gora is north from Sector South.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the Medak area is where, exactly, so that we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is village of Medak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Village of Medak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that's why this is defined like Medak -- let me see the translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because the Medak pocket is then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Medak pocket is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That may have caused my confusion, moving from Petrova Gora, which is outside of Sector South, and then the Medak area, whereas it was my understanding that the Medak pocket was, at least, not in Sector South. But apparently now you're referring to Medak village, which is to be found where, exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On the road from Gospic to Gracac, let's say about 35 to 40 kilometres north-west from Gracac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the word "Medak".

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Somewhere in the middle between Gospic and Gracac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the word "Medak" triggered my misunderstanding also in relation to the well-known Medak pocket area. Under those circumstances --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The exhibit -- let me just check again the exhibit which was assigned number -- let me just -- no, no number was yet assigned. There was no objection by Ms. Mahindaratne. Mr. Registrar, the number will be --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 3D597 will be assigned Exhibit D1931. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go through quickly the standard operative procedure for the search of the terrain, because it's been already discussed, and this is mentioned in paragraph 207 of your expert report. There, you described the procedure as taking place through seven steps. Rather than going through the description which is contained in your expert report, can you tell us if there is anything you'd like to add to your expert report, or is there anything you'd like to clarify?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should only like to say that the seven steps, as contained here, were not something that I was able to find in the documents of the special police. Rather, based on everything that was done over the period of two months in the area, and the activities undertaken, I made the conclusion that this sort of procedure was followed. The procedure could be described in five or nine steps. The important thing is that it was, in fact, adhered to -- adhered to the way it's been described. It was known to everyone, and this was the way it was implemented from the point when a decision was made of the fact that something needed to be searched to the point when, as the final step in the search, a report was sent to the chief of the Main Staff on the searches conducted during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The searches of the terrain conducted during the day were described in a report that was sent to General Markac, and General Markac then sent a report on the activities on a particular date to the Main Staff. The Chamber was able to see numerous documents reflecting the procedure. In view of what you state in paragraph 208 of your report, can you give us your comments on the position of General Markac when it came to receiving and forwarding reports on the searches of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The search of the terrain was conducted in such a way that the commander of the search operation on a day was designated, who would be assigned forces of a certain strength. They would set out from a certain line and search a given area frontally. There were two ways of approaching this. One was such that the units would set out from a line and reach a given location, as specified in the order for the searches for that day. The second possibility was that the line that was supposed to be reached would already be -- would already have certain forces present there that were supposed to take on from there, especially if the terrain was rugged. And in the event of coming across enemy forces, the enemy forces could be captured or neutralised by the forces that were engaged in the so-called blockade. Once the forces reached the final line, group leaders of the forces involved would report to the commander of the special unit of a given police administration, and these commanders would, in turn, report to the commander of the operation on all matters that were uncovered or come across. Where possible, the reports would be drafted in Gracac. When this was not possible, it was done by the commander of the operation, himself. It is -- it clearly follows from all these reports that whatever the commander of the operation wrote in his own hand, this is what was forwarded to the Main Staff. As for the position of the commander, that's to say General Markac, the first level would be the group commander, above him the commander of the special unit, above him the commander of the operation for the day, and above him -- or, rather, the fourth level of the chain of command would be General Markac, who then sent a report to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 208, you state that the format of the report which was sent to the chief of the Main Staff with General Markac's signature was the same as was the signature of the report, regardless of whether General Markac was in Gracac or in the Plitvice Lakes when the focus of the searches shifted there. You say every day it is demonstrated that the reports were identical almost 100 per cent, and your conclusion was that this meant that General Markac did not intervene in any way or seek for the reports made by the commander of the operation to be modified. Rather, he was fully confident that the information contained in these reports was correct. According to you, was it possible for General Markac, as the fourth level of the hierarchy of the chain of command you described, for him to engage in double-checking and verifying these day-to-day reports sent to him by the commanders of actions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was such a possibility for him to do that where there was any need for it. However, since these were reports made on a daily basis and which did not, in fact, contain any controversial elements, in terms of events not having been fully described or in terms of the use of ambiguous formulations or unequivocal formulations, and since the documentation accompanying day-to-day searches was quite voluminous, and since there also exist handwritten reports and reports which were sent encoded to the Main Staff, they are a clear indication of the fact that there were no modifications made to them. General Markac could have supplemented the information contained in these reports with certain information that was not directly linked to the searches carried out on the day. However, the fact of the matter was that General Markac was fully confident that the commanders engaged or commanding these search operations were up to scratch and that what was written there was accurate. In the military and the police practice, it is customary for every document to bear the signature of the commander at the bottom. Since the documents were sent encrypted or encoded, these documents did not contain a handwritten signature, but the signature, in terms of the name being printed of the commander, was there. Regardless of whether General Markac was present in a given area on the day or not, the reports were sent bearing his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You go on to state in your expert report the chronology of the activities of the special police units between the 21st of August and the 9th of October, in and outside of the area of Sector South. I don't want to engage in an exercise of going through all these activities on a daily basis. I would merely like to indicate your conclusion, where you state that it was more than 5.000 square kilometres of areas covered by these search operations. And you go on to state that the overall search operations undertaken by the special police force were characterised by only two incidents. This was in paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This was a search operation that was carried out by the same units, but you say this should not lead to a conclusion that the system was not workable and that it involved a lack of discipline on the part of the members involved?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The number you referred to as a paragraph number was not caught by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I can see now. This is the paragraph number 259.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: General, sir, can you give us your comments on the conclusions you draw in this paragraph of your expert report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the search operation of Petrova Gora was the first one to be conducted which did not -- or, rather, the mop-up operation was carried out first, and there were no incidents, and then the search operation began on the 21st of August and ended on the 9th of October, had the policemen been told that they could freely engage in the search operation as they willed, without adhering to any rules or regulations, then the number of such incidents, as it were, would certainly have been much higher. And had the circumstances prevailed the way I described them just now, then such incidents would have been recorded on the very first day. We saw that the two incidents were -- occurred on the 25th and the 26th, that's to say four days into the search operation. We saw that the unit involved was the same in both incidents, and we saw that neither before nor after the two incidents did other incidents occur. The way in which the commander prepared the forces in Gracac and the way he instructed them with regard to the activity, he certainly did not advise anyone to violate any rules or regulations, but rather to engage in the operation in the way prescribed in the relevant manuals and in keeping with the practice of the work of the special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And my final question, General, sir. You went through a great number of different sorts of documents in preparing your expert report. Did you come across a document which related to the work of the special police where you noted an unlawful order or a report which indicated that there was unlawful conduct recorded on the part of the members of the special police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the documentation that was available to me, I did not come across a single such document, either an order, or a report, or any other sort of document which would involve, either on the part of the Main Staff or any of the structures subordinated to it, or either on the part of the military districts, ordinary or military police force, where the special police would be referred to as a party which played any role in the commission of crime. I also did not come across a single special police document which would in any way refer to or open up a possibility for condoning or even encourage such conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Though I did say that that was to be my final question, I have another question for you, General, sir. We can see from your expert report that during Operation Storm and in its aftermath, you were not present in the area. During the Homeland War, before or after, did you have any professional or personal contacts with General Markac, and do you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During Operation Storm, I was a colonel, and General Markac was colonel general. I was predominantly working in various staffs or within the educational system, so I did not have any encounters with General Markac, and I cannot say that I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answers. Your Honour, I have completed my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Before we take a break, could I -- could we briefly have a look at page 24, line 18, where you invited us to look at document 3D00226, a report referred to in footnote 158, which was -- you read, more or less, into the record what we find in paragraph 201 of the report. I think this was given the number D1930. Could we have a look at D1930 at this moment? Could we get that on the screen? If I search for D1930, I get something different, so therefore I wondered whether there was any -- I don't know, Mr. Registrar, whether you searched on the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In my searches, I had a technical problem. I got something different on my screen. I now see that there is no problem there, because one of the -- I had difficulties in getting the right report on my screen. In view of my earlier questions in relation to what was within and what was outside Sector South, I wanted to verify whether this was, as I meanwhile found for the village of Medak, that it's within the report in the relevant paragraph, no place is mentioned there, and I wanted just to verify whether we are within or outside the territorial scope of Sector South. Could you assist me, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. You can see in the middle of that report that the place where these events -- the village that these events took place is the village of Skrbic, and in the brackets it's written "Mazin," so this is the area within inside of Sector South.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We're now talking about Mazin being north-east of Gracac in the direction of Donji Lapac; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because I didn't find any reference in the report, but this clearly situates this event in Sector South. Yes, thank you. I have now better read the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could I have an exhibit number for the report, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For which report now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The expert's report of Mr. General Repinc, which is 3D00993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The expert report. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Since it's the whole of the expert report - I'm looking at the other parties, but apparently there are no objections - Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document will be assigned Exhibit D1932. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and it is marked for identification at this moment. We will finally decide. It's always better to know everything about -- to have heard the whole of the examination, including cross-examination, before we finally decide on admission. But until now, there's nothing, I think, which would oppose admission into evidence, but let's wait for a while. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: God bless you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The fact that you're on your feet suggests that the Gotovina Defence will cross-examine Mr. Repinc first?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Repinc, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kehoe is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, General. I would just like to ask you a few questions about some items in your report. I'd like to start off with your beginning section, and starting off on paragraph 29 where you talk about the directive of the chief of the General Staff in 1992 which had a general -- an overall intent for the liberation of the occupied areas of the Republic of Croatia. And in paragraph 30, you note that the directive from the General Staff was accepted and adopted at a session of the Defence and National Security Council, VONS, at the beginning of 1992. Now, General, you were aware of the existence and of the function of VONS, were you not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me turn your attention to paragraph 36 of your report, where you note that the final decision -- I'd just like to clear up this area, by the way, General. In paragraph 36, you note that the final decision to carry out Operation Storm was made by the commander-in-chief, Franjo Tudjman, in Brioni on 31 July 1995. General, this Trial Chamber has received testimony from Ambassador Zuzul, an attendee at the VONS meeting on the 3rd of August of 1995, and I'm referring to D1485 at paragraph 20 where Ambassador Zuzul noted that the final decision on launching the military operation for liberation was brought on the VONS session on 3 August 1995. He also testified to that same matter on page 18304, the line that begins with my question on line 13, but it's just a reiteration of what I've just read to you, but also another member -- special assistant to the president, Vesna Skare Ozbolt, noted the same thing in D1471 at paragraph 8. Now, General, you were aware that the final decision to move ahead with Operation Storm was, in fact, not made until the VONS meeting on the 3rd of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wrote here, I was looking at it from an exclusively military aspect. So on Brioni, the basic concept was adopted, how Operation Storm was to be carried out in such a way as to defend the east and the south and attack operations in the other parts, offensive operations. So it was -- the decision was made, as I understood it, to go into action. However, on Brioni, the decision wasn't made as to when this would happen. That decision was made on the 3rd, after the negotiations in Geneva fell through. And had that not been the case, then the chief of the Main Staff would not have been able, on the 3rd, to issue an order for going ahead with Operation Storm. So what we're dealing with here is that from the military aspects for the preparations of the operation, everything was decided, the preparations were decided on, but I can only assume that if the Geneva negotiations had been successful, then a decision wouldn't have been made at the council meeting on the 3rd, nor would the chief of staff, on the 3rd in the afternoon, issue his order to launch the operation on the morning of the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I want to shift topics, if we may. And, General, just bear with me. My cross-examination will be covering several topics and will not be the type of testimony that you engaged in with Mr. Mikulicic. So just bear with me, and I'd just like to turn to another topic, and that had to do with the preparation of the defence or the status of the enemy, and that is -- if I can, in paragraphs 77 and 78 of your report. And yesterday you told us at page 26703, line 22 -- beginning on line 22, you said: "What one needs to say, in view of the organisation of that army and those who are in command, it is that the army exclusively applied the doctrine of the former Yugoslavia." Now, the army that you're talking about that applied the doctrine of the former Yugoslavia was the ARSK; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continuing on: "And on that basis, they applied all the rules and instructions and documents referred to the use of military units in combat, in defence, or assault."

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, in your report you cite D944. And if we could bring 944 up on the screen, D944. Now, this is, as it says on the front cover page, a directive for the use of the Serbian Army of Krajina. And if we could go to paragraph 5.11. That's about 15 pages in, in the English. That's it at the bottom in the English. Now, General, focusing on point 9 -- 11, you note in your report at paragraph 77 and 78, that what the Army of the Republic of Serb Krajina set forth in this document at paragraph 5.11 was simply a reiteration or an articulation of the same philosophy that was set forth in the JNA manual that you talked about in D919 [sic]; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, because in the manuals which defined combat deployment of the units of the Yugoslav Army, it was precisely defined and stated that populated areas must -- it doesn't say "can," but "must be include into the defence system."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We'll talk about a few specifics about the defence of populated areas in one moment, but I'm interested in the sequence that we have here. JNA doctrine set forth a certain policy on the defence of populated areas that was then followed by the Republic of Serb Krajina, and the commander at the time of Operation Storm was a former JNA officer, General Mrksic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. Your Honour, just a slight correction of the transcript. In the line 39 -- in the page 39, line 22, it's mentioned "D919," instead of 1919. That's the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel. If I misspoke in that regard, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I believe not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Oh, okay. Counsel is 100 per cent right, it is 1919.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This has been corrected. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So going back to my question, General, the person that was following this JNA doctrine through until August of 1995 was a former JNA officer, General Mrksic; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, but he wasn't a former; he was an active officer of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine, sir. But let's talk about what the populated areas were, and let's look at that paragraph 5.11. If we could flip back on the English, if we could, because we have something on the bottom of the page before we flip over to the next page. In B/C/S, it's fine. If we could just go back one page. Thank you. Thank you. Now, on the bottom of that page, if you can see that, General, we talk about: "In the defence zones of the corps and brigades, immediately begin preparations of larger populated areas and towns for long-term and circular defence ..." Now, what does that mean, General? What does that mean, preparing these populated areas for long-term and circular defence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that all approaches to the town, if I can use that expression, must be secured in engineering terms, that is to say, that fortification must be constructed for protection and for combat, which means that the area must be secured with obstacles to prevent the enemy from passing through certain axes or to channel the enemy towards certain areas where they would be routed with artillery weapons or other means, which means that in addition to the approaches to town, the axes to the town, the town must be secured for defence too, which in the classical sense means, that each and every facility and building becomes a sort of mini-fortress, fortification, and that forces should be designated to fight in those areas, especially when it is assumed that armoured, mechanised forces will be used against the town. So that means to prepare either permanent mine obstacles or to assign forces in charge of neutralising and attacking enemy forces. So it means an all-out comprehensive preparation of the terrain to make it impregnable and ready for defence, and as we used to say, that to the very last man, the very last man should have this assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's go one step further on the "very last man" theory. And if we could turn the page in English, and leave it on that page in B/C/S. It notes that -- at the top of the page and the bottom of the page in -- at the top of the page in English and the bottom of the page in B/C/S: "Engage the entire able-bodied population, Civilian Protection units, SVK command and units in the preparation. "Focus on the preparation of towns and populated areas on the front-lines and the preparation of the town of Knin, for which a command and defence units shall be established separately." And in your testimony yesterday, at page 2706, you noted that these populated areas would, to quote line 3: "... would be the basic focal point for the defence." Now, could you just elaborate on that a bit, especially with regard to Knin, that based on the JNA philosophy, which you as a former JNA officer are familiar with, where does Knin fall into this structure, and how do you equate it as the focal point of the defence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when it comes to Knin, it's clear to one and all that we're dealing with a town which was the symbol -- a symbol, in fact. And it's also clear to everyone that if you have a symbol, something that represents a concept around which the population and the army can rally, then when the symbol falls, all the other elements fall, too, within the concept of defence. So in that sense, Knin, as the focal point, as the center of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, both as a political and military central point, is something that must be defended, absolutely, and defended successfully, because should a town like that fall, then it would have a terrible effect on the moral and psychological level. It would have very negative repercussions on the entire defence system and the conduct of the population and the army alike.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Taking it one step further to Knin itself, and moving past its symbolic nature, and let's discuss the fact that it was the location of the headquarters of the Main Staff of the Army of Serb Krajina, and I'd like to discuss with you your testimony yesterday at page 26706, beginning at line 6, where you noted: "Now, when speaking of command posts, I should like to mention that similarly it was expressly required that the command post be located next to logistics, or a logistics company be attached to a command post, or logistics company with all its basic elements, that is to say, the command and communication system, the support wings and so on, which, in fact, led to the fact that should there be an attack launched against the populated area, it would be impossible not to target and not to act against these elements for the simple reason that this was the very basis of every defence system, to destroy the system of command and control and supervision and communications." Now, by way of clarification, when you note in here that this was the very basis of every defence system, what are you talking about, General? What is the "this"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we talk about control or command posts, sometimes it is thought that it is a command bunker or command vehicle and that it is a small facility of that nature which, once it is destroyed, the whole problem is resolved. However, command post and the system of control and command from that post is not only that; it is much more. It's clear to everybody that the system of command and control is something that must function continuously, which means that a system of that kind must be defended and protected at all times, and it must have all the elements which enable a commander to function normally. So a command post is not only the commander and his staff and headquarters, but everything else, all the support elements which enable that commander and his staff to function normally or, in other words, to supervise combat. So in that sense, it means all the elements which a command structure must have, must necessarily have, logistics included, because it must function and work normally. So it implies systems and units of communication which must also be engaged for the unit or, rather, the command to be able to establish a system of command and control, and reporting and monitoring, and all the other subsystems that are set up and needed during combat, and of course it must have its protective elements to protect and defend the command in case of an attack against it, which can be a military police unit or military police units or other units which can be deployed separately depending on the level of the command involved and which can be deployed and used and engaged for the protection of a command post. So a command post is not exclusively one building and one commander within that building, but it implies an entire system, which takes up much more space than a mere building or just a building in which the commander functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, let's just wrap this area up with this question: In the mind of a reasonable commander, such as General Gotovina, getting ready to launch Operation Storm, would a reasonable commander, such as General Gotovina, have a firm basis of believing that in a town such as Knin, which is the focal point for the defence of the Republic of Serb Krajina, and that it was going to engage the entire population in that defence, and that it was the center for the Army of the Republic of Serb Krajina, in that its headquarters were there, would it be reasonable for a commander to believe that that particular town was going to be defended strongly should it be attacked?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to that question. This is now going into facts as to what General Gotovina would have decided or not have decided, and this witness -- Mr. Kehoe has not established the foundation for this witness to respond to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that what expectations arise from -- systemic considerations is a question you can put to an expert witness, not to a witness of fact. Now, you can ask such questions about reasonable commanders. There was some comment included there as well that Mr. Gotovina was a reasonable commander, which is, of course, testimony given by you, Mr. Kehoe, at this moment. So, therefore, if we are talking in the abstract, if we are talking about what one could expect if a certain system was in place, or whether it was factually in place, or whether it was on paper in place, of course, could still make a difference. I think, as a matter of fact, that we are talking at this moment about -- mainly about what was designed to be there, and that's a question you can put to an expert witness. So, therefore, the witness may answer the question and should ignore the comments elements in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, my apologies. I should not have included that, and it should have been just a question "the reasonable commander" without a name attached to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can you answer that question, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can answer that question. I think that given the circumstances and in normal planning, every commander, regardless of whether he was reasonable or not, would assume that a town like that would defend itself with all available means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, if I may just shift gears for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness said "given the circumstances." He has not explained what these circumstances were. As I pointed out earlier, that the question was put in a rather abstract manner, and, of course, I don't think you would disagree with me that circumstances could give strong contraindications as well - I'm not saying that there were anyway - but therefore if the witness refers to "given the circumstances," I'd like to know what circumstances he had on his mind. Mr. Repinc, could you tell us what exactly you refer to when you said "given the circumstances"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I meant the situation in general. And when we're speaking about circumstances, it is a fact that Knin was what it was at that time, for Serbian Krajina. It's also a fact that - and this common knowledge from all the other decisions and talks - that the operation had to be completed as quickly as possible, in the shortest space of time. So once an order was given that it should last as short a time as possible, then that the most important points in the defence system of a given army should be destroyed as soon as possible, although that might present a problem because those facilities would be best defended as well. So in that sense, along those lines, that's what I considered to be the circumstances; that is to say, that Knin was the capital, the center of political and military power, and that the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia had, in the shortest space of time, to carry out the operation and reach the borders. And this could only be done if the focus of attention, the focus of the rebellion, was destroyed as soon as possible, and that meant Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, may I just -- Mr. Repinc, the question was about what you could expect as far as defence is concerned. I asked you what circumstances you had considered when you gave that answer, and in your explanation it comes down to an answer to quite a different question, whether what was done in taking, or liberating, whatever you call it, Knin was well done, and moved away from the question that was put to you. I just want you and also the parties to know that this is what I observe at this time as a point of logic and explanation, that it is at least a bit confusing that when you explain your answer, you give an answer to a rather different question. And I think it's sometimes good that if such confusion comes up to my mind, that I do not conceal that from the parties. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I just ask an additional question to clarify this yet further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I can go back to your answer to my question, General, you noted at page 46, line 9, that: "I think that given the circumstances and normal planning, every commander, regardless of whether he was reasonable or not, would assume that a town like that would defend itself with all available means." I think that given the circumstances that was -- issue that was raised by the Presiding Judge was: What are those circumstances that would lead any reasonable commander to believe that this town was going to be defended with all available means?
