That, I believe, is the inquiry that the Chamber would like to pursue with you; not what happened afterwards, but what, in the eyes of a reasonable commander, would be those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I'm not saying that the witness did not answer my question, but that the follow-up -- in the follow-up he established a link with a totally different question. So, therefore, I think the witness explained - that's at least how I understood it - that the central -- the political and symbolic -- the central position of Knin as, I would say, the focal point for the RSK, that that were circumstances which would create the expectation that it would be firmly defended. That's how I understood your answer, and then you followed up with something of a different nature. Did I understand your answer well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. I have to confirm that whoever supposed that a town like Knin, which was a center of political, military, and other sort of power, would not be fully prepared for defence would start from a completely erroneous premise. Whenever preparations are conducted, and in relation to matters that are not certain, preparations have to be somewhat based on assumptions that will then partly be or be not confirmed in the course of the action. Those that are confirmed true are facts, and those that are confirmed wrong are dismissed, and the armed operation conducted by a certain force is readjusted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, shifting just slightly to your testimony concerning Gracac and the axis of attack of the special police, and you noted on page 26714, lines 1 through 15, the importance of Gracac as a crossroads from -- leading towards Gospic to Obrovac towards Benkovac, and then also the road -- crossroads leading to Knin, given the essential nature of the crossroads going through Gracac, it would be reasonable for a commander under these circumstances to shell those crossroads to suppress movement by enemy troops, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One last area of inquiry, General, and I'd like to turn to paragraph 96 and 97 of your report. And in 96 and 97, you discuss General Cervenko's order in D279. If we could bring that up briefly on the screen. And this is the order that discusses the operative borders between, for instance, the Split Military District and the Gospic Military District, and other military districts. Now, you recall this order setting out the particular areas for the line of demarcation between the Gospic Military District and the Split Military District. And if we could turn to the map on D280. Now, General, this is the map received in evidence that plots the grid coordinates that are set forth in D279, and this is the map that you and I discussed when you were kind enough to chat with me for a bit the other night. Do you recall this, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me just shift for one moment to yet another document, and you do discuss this document in your report, but it doesn't necessarily address this particular point, and that's D559. It is the 14 August 1995 order by General Cervenko. You discussed this order, in fact, in item 198 of your report, but I'd like to discuss it in this context. And if we could bring 558 on. D558, please. That's it. And this is the order, if we can go to the paragraph B, and in the English it's on the second page, that deals with some of the orders concerning the use of home guards and local units to clear up areas. But I would like to -- excuse me, I'm sorry, D559. I apologise, D559. I misspoke. If you go to page 2 in the English, this is the document, General, where you were talking about clearing up of the terrain, but I would like to talk about some other aspects of this document that have to do with changing the zones of responsibility of the Split Military District and the Gospic Military District. And if we could turn to page 6 in the English and page 4 in the B/C/S. Now, if we just look at this with regard to the Gospic Military District, there is a level -- a zone of responsibility that's set forth. And if we could turn to the next page in the English, that same page in the B/C/S, we see another area of responsibility set forth for the Split Military District. And we saw just briefly what the zones of responsibility were in Exhibit D280, and I'd like to just -- with your assistance, General, and your expertise, I'd like to just plot this change in areas of responsibility after the 14th of August, 1995, and I'd like to bring up 1D3052, and I want to show you a series of charts on this score. If I may, by way of clarification, Mr. President, I do not have this in B/C/S. However, the witness does speak English and read English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there seems to be no major problem, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would please verify whether he has any difficulties in understanding certain matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, I know you and I when we were chatting the other night spoke in English. If you have any problem with anything here in the English language, please let us know. Now, what we have here, I have mapped off in blue what we have previously in Exhibit 278 -- excuse me, 279 and D280, which was the area of responsibilities after the 6th of August. And just plotting out the change in those areas in D559, I have the red line. And I can show you a sequence here so you may be able to orient yourself just a little bit more. We can turn to -- I can go through all these maps, and then we can just ask a few questions from here. If we can turn to the next map, which is 1D -- well, we have it at the next page. Just the next page, if we can. This is the same map as you can -- with the orders, but we will put it in with the confrontation line as well as the international border. If we go to the next page. We could spin that, if we could. General, this is just a similar view from a different topographical map or more elevated topographical map showing the line of confrontation in the two areas. And if we can just go to the last map. We can spin that. General, what this is is just an overlay of the order in 14 August 1995 from the Main Staff, D559, and this is -- the red overlay is on the map that you saw previously in D280, which was as of the 6th of August. So, General, what we see here is an expansion of the area for the Gospic Military District after the 14th of August, 1995, and obviously concomitantly a cutting down of the area of responsibility in Croatia, at least, for the Split Military District in 14 August 1995. Now, General, at this period of time most of the troops for the Split Military District -- and if we could just -- were moving towards the confrontation line against the VRS when -- the other Serb forces, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume so, on the basis of what I studied, that that was the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go back to the second map. Now, if we look at the confrontation line here, what this depicts is a significant larger area of responsibility on the confrontation line with the VRS for the Split Military District and much less responsibility in the confrontation with the VRS for the Gospic Military District; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell because the line, as it has been shown here, I can only see the line of confrontation as of the 13th of August. However, based on the fact that at the time the attack began, which was the 4th of August, the boundaries of the military districts were applied that had been established by the supreme commander back in 1993, they did not change at the start of the operation. They did not change until the 6th of August, when the chief of the Main Staff issued a fresh order defining areas of responsibility. However, I have to say that the reason why the 6th of August order was cited here lay in the very fact that the area of responsibility between -- or, rather, the boundary between the two military districts changed on the 6th of August. General Markac, who participated in the operation and was present on the boundary between the two districts, was not privy to the order, which clearly follows from the fact that later on, on the 8th, he expressly asked the chief of the Main Staff to be told precisely what the boundary was. This shows that he was not privy to the 6th of August order defining the boundaries. I read the entire order, but I did not quote the parts that I did not believe that were relevant to my expert report. Why didn't I quote the change in the boundaries? Well, because at that stage there were no more combat activities and the change in boundary did not have any relevance for the special forces. The fact of the matter is that on the 14th, there was a change. Gracac was taken back to the Gospic Military District. This was shown through the fact that the 188th Home Guards Regiment was told it should go back to Gracac. However, the 14th of August order which was issued to military districts was not sent to General Markac, either. The point in me quoting it was that I wanted to indicate that the order spoke of both search operation and mop-up operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, General, your quote in there. I was using the order to show these changes in boundaries as of the 14th. And you have no dispute that there was, in fact, a change in boundaries on the 14th of August; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we'll offer into evidence 1D3052.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have principally any objections to admission, but may I be just given some time to study this? I have just received the map just to the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document will be marked for identification. We'll hear from you then later. Mr. Registrar, the number which this document will be marked is --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D1933. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Keep that status forthwith.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, just for the sake of having fewer exhibits, I put the four maps in as one exhibit, the four pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then the four maps. We'll then hear the position of the Prosecution on this exhibit, all four maps.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just clarifying your last answer, General, and I think it is a bit confusing. You do agree that there was a change of boundaries based on General Cervenko's order of the 14th of August, 1995; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kay, will it be you who will cross-examine Mr. Repinc?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Repinc, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay is counsel for Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Repinc, I'm just going to ask you a few questions, and it concerns paragraph 222 of your report. It's page 94 in the English, Your Honour, and it concerns a document, Exhibit D99. And perhaps if we can have that on the screen, please. Have you got the passage in your report, Mr. Repinc?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in this passage of your report, you're dealing with a number of reports or information that General Cermak distributes to various parties concerning activities of the special police that were planned, or what they did, and you refer to the fact that not always the addressees are the same on each document. Do you recollect this passage?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but I think it wasn't General Cermak who sent them, but General Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I said "General Markac," actually, and I think it was translated or heard wrongly. But you're quite right. If we just look at Exhibit D99, then. Can you see it on your screen? Have a look at this document. It's dated the 28th of August. It's the report from General Markac to General Cervenko. It concerns assignments on the 28th of August, and we can see on the first page the activities that are described and the area they were operating around the village of Unista, Podinarje, Mount Dinara, with the objective of finding broken sabotage and terrorist enemy groups as well as materiel, technical equipment. And in each section, section 1, the various special police forces are described as to their activities. And in paragraph 2, we see the Zadar-Knin special police who were operating on that day; page 2 in the English. And in this document, Mr. Repinc, you can see the activities of the Zadar-Knin police in this paragraph, what they did, and they came across a number of persons, including what is described as enemy soldiers. And we see various names in that section; Nenad Todorovic, Milan Todorovic, other names which I won't cite out, but the Court is familiar with this document. And on this occasion, a man called Mr. Roberts, who was the press officer for UNCRO, and other UNCRO officials were involved with these enemy soldiers and were there when the special police discovered them, and arrangements were made for the hand-over of these soldiers so that it could be monitored by UNCRO. Firstly, are you familiar with the background to this particular incident?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From the reports that the special police drafted, I merely stated that the elements -- I merely stated the elements that were specific for the search operation carried on that day. They had to do with clashes with the enemy forces that were come across, about the civilian persons, amounts of ammunition or types of weaponry found, about the fact whether the civilians had already been registered or not, whether they were handed over to someone or not, whether, among the persons who were found there, there were individuals registered or merely turned over to other parties. In that sense, I did not go into the nature of the event on that day or into the incidents that may have occurred on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There was discussion earlier today about clashes, about the capturing of enemy soldiers, and one matter that was not mentioned was surrendering in this form of enemy soldiers and the involvement of the international community. Were you aware, during the writing of your expertise, of that particular feature that happened during the clearing-up operations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Truth be told, I could not state on the basis of the reports I reviewed, that there were individuals who actually surrendered. "Surrender" means that an individual approaches you before you approach him. In the majority of the cases, certain individuals were found in a given area. Can this be regarded as an act of surrender, the very fact that the individual did not put up armed resistance? Well, that's a different aspect of the matter altogether. I would not consider it to be similar to surrender. I would consider as surrender an individual who would come out of hiding or out of his shelter and approach me, and not the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we just look at another document, then, Exhibit D1100, 1100. This is another report from General Markac to General Cervenko on the 24th of August, again describing the activities of the special police forces. Do you have it amongst your papers there, Mr. Repinc? I want you to look at it. It's a report on completed tasks for the 23rd of August. It sets out the activities in paragraph 1 of the Krapina-Zagorje Police Administration Special Police, and in section 2 it sets out the activities of the Karlovac Police Administration Special Police. And we can see here that at the village of Radakovic, a number of elderly civilians were found. The village of Duboki Dol is mentioned as being a place where 15 camouflage uniforms were found, which according to the elderly local civilians were left there by members of the enemy formations who had changed into civilian clothing and then surrendered to UNCRO representatives. Firstly, am I right in saying this is a document that you would have seen during your work on your expert report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In this paragraph here, written by General Markac obviously on information transmitted to him, it is describing here 15 camouflage uniforms and members of the enemy forces who had changed into civilian clothing and then surrendered to UNCRO representatives. Just looking at this specific passage again, did that form any part of your expertise dealing with this issue of surrender by the forces of the ARSK during the clearing-up operations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen the document, and it was quoted just like all the others, and this surrender too, as far as I remember. Let me just take a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is about this trend of the surrendering of enemy forces to UNCRO that I want to ask you about, because it involves the internationals rather than just the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is -- well, what it says about surrender, whether they surrendered and to whom -- in military terminology, you don't surrender to somebody who is not a party in the conflict and who is not attacking you or who has not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let me just cut you there. It's not that I'm interested in definitions. I'm just interested in this trend of enemy soldiers giving themselves up, going to UNCRO, to internationals, and providing themselves that way to the Croatian authorities; not definitions, but just this feature which we have seen in just these two reports that we've looked at. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand, and quite obviously part of those forces did surrender to the representatives of the international forces or, rather, UNCRO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to the activities of the special police, whereby in some cases the ARSK forces went to the internationals to declare themselves, were you aware that there had been a discussion and a procedure agreed between the UNCRO commander and General Cermak about this trend about the surrender in this way? For the Court's reference, Exhibit P378. I saw Your Honour looking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was mainly raising my eyebrows in view of the use of the word "trend," but I didn't say anything. But since you're referring to my looking, I will explain to you what was on my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's whether two swallows make a summer or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm trying to deal with this without getting too bogged down in paperwork for a fairly simple issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware that this was happening?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to this question. This witness is testifying on the basis of documents he has reviewed and analysed, and Mr. Kay's question is more factual, Were you aware that this was happening?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness -- there are three options. First, that he's not aware; second, that he is aware on the basis of the documents; third, that he is aware, but not based on documents, but on any other source of knowledge. And I think Mr. Kay is entitled to explore whether this witness can answer any of these questions. And from these three options it may be clear to you that, of course, the Chamber will carefully look at what the source of knowledge of the witness in this respect is, if there is any knowledge. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as that is concerned, during my preparations I read a large number of -- read through a large number of documents, and among others I came across this particular reference, that is to say, the problem that occurred and the complaints Mr. Cermak had to make against the international community with respect to this kind of practice. But this was not part of my expert report or expertise, nor did I deal with it, nor did I consider it to be relevant for the functioning of the special police in the search operations of the terrain. But, yes, I have read through that, but I did not attach any great importance in compiling my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said "complaints Mr. Cermak had to make against the international community with respect to this kind of practice." Is that what you meant? If so, please identify what complaints. Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I termed them complaints. Now, whether Mr. Cermak would explain this in a different way or not, I really can't remember. But I do know that there were discussions and that General Cermak considered that the members of the opposing forces should surrender to the Croatian authorities and not to UNCRO. So that's what I can say on the basis of what I read. Now, whether they were complaints, objections, or protests, or whatever, or some other form of communication, it's difficult for me to say that now. I gave a free interpretation of that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you read any of the UNCRO documents where this matter was discussed between General Forand, commander of UNCRO forces, and General Cermak as to the procedure that was to take place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you read any of the documents? That was my question, not whether you could confirm, but whether you had read any of the other sources of information.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer went along the lines of saying that I can't say whether I read any documents like that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The reason that General Cermak was then being copied in from the 28th of August as to some of the activities on some of the days of the special police, were you aware, was because of the need to inform the international community, UNCRO, as to what was taking place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were to say that, then I would have assumed, I would have been making an assumption that that was the main reason. All I can say and confirm is that the practice was that reports were exclusively sent to the chief of the Main Staff, and then that practice was changed whereby the reports were sent not only to him, but were also sent out to the minister of the interior and to General Cermak, as the commander of the Knin Military District, and also to the commanders of the military districts of Split and Gospic, which means to all those people who were located in Sector South, except the chief and the minister, of course, who -- well, the chief had to receive reports from General Markac about his activities, as he did from everybody else in the chain of command. And the minister appeared from time to time. I don't know why he would receive reports on some occasions and not on others. But, anyway, I think that the normal, standard practice was that those who were in a certain area knew what was going on in that area, either for that particular day or for the following day, because General Markac also sent out information about what his units would be doing the following day, what areas they would search the following day. Now, whether that was supposed to be sent to General Cermak or not, I can't speculate about that. I don't know why General Cermak was included in the list, for what reason. But, anyway, from that day onwards the reports were, indeed, sent to those addressees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you mean to say "Knin Military District"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN REPINC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said "Knin Garrison," "Knin Garrison."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I've got no further question to ask you. Your Honour, on this subject there is a single document which we would like to put into evidence that's relevant to this issue, which is something that the Court has been aware of. It is 2D00068. It's on our disclosure list. It seems a bit heavy, if I may put it that way, to put a formal Bar table for a single document which might be dealt with quite simply now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That purpose may be served by an explanation at this moment from you, and then we'll hear from Ms. Mahindaratne whether that would cause her any problems to make up her mind as to whether or not to object to the document. And if it's a short document, and where it's clear on the record what the reason -- what the relevant portions of the document are, then that might -- I'm also looking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has no difficulties in deciding on admission of that document. Could we have it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's on the screen. It's a short two-pager. It's an UNCRO document from Colonel Tymchuk dated the 29th of August addressed to the Croatian Army liaison officer in Knin, and it concerns the matters that we have looked at in D99. And that is why -- the content of the report in D99. And, in fact, if the second page of this document is now shown, the names I mentioned on the transcript 10 minutes ago, Nenad Todorovic, Milan Todorovic, linked to that document D99. It was something I came across last night and thought that it might be helpful as an extra document on this matter. I hope the Prosecution have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, this seems to be a document to which --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- further establishes the practice that apparently on that date, in relation to these persons, took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be assigned Exhibit D1934. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1934 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm grateful to my learned friend, and that finishes my matters, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Ms. Mahindaratne, I think the Prosecution was granted leave to start cross-examination on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that since there are no other witnesses available, Mr. Mikulicic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's correct. We have only one witness left, and he will come to The Hague after the testimony of Mr. Repinc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us already an indication as to how much time your cross-examination would take, Ms. Mahindaratne?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I believe, Mr. President, about three sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About three sessions. So that would do for most if not all of the Monday, and we'll then see whether there's any need for re-examination, which means that we can temporarily let the witness go, although he -- Mr. Repinc, the Prosecution has asked to be allowed to start cross-examination only on Monday. Earlier, we had an expectation that most of the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination by the other Defence teams would bring us well into Friday. This now turns out to be not the case. First of all, I do not know what you expected and to what extent you were informed about cross-examination by the Prosecution to start only on Monday and whether you are available on Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was told that the cross-examination would be starting on Monday and that it would last a certain number of days during the following week, and so I have adjusted my personal schedule to that. So I am available for testimony on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have a few procedural matters to deal with, but they are of no concern to you. Therefore, I would already like to allow you to leave the courtroom, and I would like to inform you that we would like to see you back on Monday, the 18th. If you would please -- one second, one second. We would like to see you back Monday at 9.00 in the morning. The hearing will be held in this same courtroom. And I would also like to instruct you, as I did yesterday, that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether it is testimony you've given already yesterday and today or whether that is testimony still to be given next week. As you may have heard, the expectation is that if we would not finish on Monday, that then almost for sure we would finish your -- we would conclude your examination on Tuesday. You're invited to follow the usher, and we would like to see you back on Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are a few procedural matters I would like to deal with after the break. It will not take much time, but we'll first have a break. And we'll resume -- yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to advise the Chamber that if we could, after the break, address a Bar table submission I believe we circulated two days ago. We sent it to Chambers and to Mr. Registrar, as well as all parties. The Excel spreadsheet with comments has already been completed with the Prosecution. It just needs approval from the Chamber, and then we would file the comments with the Chamber's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's put on the record. I think we can deal with that after the break. Are the parties ready yet to make their further submissions in relation to the issue of appropriateness of interviewers being close to historical events to play a role in interviewing? I think the -- you were informed that the Prosecution would have an opportunity to further reply and that both parties would have 10 minutes because we might find time for that after the break as well. Mr. Waespi, I'm looking at you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The short answer is no. We just had an exchange of e-mails with Mr. Misetic on discovery issues, and we just completed that, and we would like to postpone these arguments to Monday on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We're ready, Mr. President. But if the Prosecution's not, then we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It might not be wise to force them into them at this moment. And to schedule a hearing for those 20 minutes only tomorrow might be a bit overdone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we will not. We'll look at any further procedural matters during the break. Perhaps in view of the time, we should take 25 minutes. So we resume at 1.00 for some procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, before we deal with any other procedural matters, there was something about Bar table submissions you'd like to address. Please feel free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We circulated a Bar table submission, and all the parties have commented. It is in the spreadsheet which we sent to Mr. Registrar and the Trial Chamber, and we move to have those admitted into evidence and have them be given exhibit numbers. And then we will file the comments with the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I must admit that we -- I haven't seen it, and I think neither have my colleagues. We'll consider the matter. And perhaps this is the right moment to announce to the parties that next week when we've heard the testimony of the last witness, the Trial Chamber intends to schedule then a housekeeping session in which we'll deal with all the remaining MFIs, et cetera, and to see whether there are any loose ends which need attention before we take the next steps in this case. Therefore, the parties should then prepare for being available after the last witness to attend such housekeeping sessions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is, of course, separate from the other matter, which is the not-in-court session but the -- about the 54 bis issue. That, of course, is a bit separate, but, of course, will also take place. Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I just wish to inform the Court, so that we can close this matter, that the Prosecution has no objection to D1933, the four maps, to be entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I wanted to consult the transcript, but the number does not appear clearly. Could you repeat the number, Ms. Mahindaratne?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: D1933, Mr. President. There were four maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Four maps, D1933, until now marked for identification, are admitted into evidence. Is there any other matter we can deal with in public session, because I have one matter to deal with in private session. If not, we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Any other matter to be raised at this moment? If not, we adjourn, and we resume on Monday, the 18th of January, 9.00 in the morning, in this same Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 18th day of January, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
